description: The affordance that injects an "App settings" control into the Control UI's sidebar footer, and the host bridge it calls to open the app's own settings surface. This file is the ONE owner of that injected script: core/app-settings-affordance.js reads it (the desktop reads that module and installs the script into the gateway page over executeJavaScript; the iOS client bundles THIS FILE and installs it through a WKUserScript), so there is one copy of the injected script in the tree rather than one per client. The desktop and the phone run identical bytes; only the host bridge differs, and only in how it is wired.
why: The Control UI is upstream and its DOM is free to change at any release, so the affordance is DEFENSIVE by construction. It locates the footer by a stable selector, falls back to the footer bar and then to a fixed corner if the exact node is gone, and every step is wrapped so a change to the host page cannot throw into it. A Control UI update must be able to move the footer without breaking the page or stranding app settings.

The affordance never reimplements settings: it only opens the shared surface, by calling a host bridge the client installs. That bridge is the ONE thing that differs between clients: the desktop points `__clawAppSettings.open` at an IPC that runs openSettings(), and the phone points it at a WKScriptMessageHandler that raises its sheet.

The bridge global and the CONFIG global are two different names on purpose. The desktop installs its bridge through Electron's contextBridge, which exposes a FROZEN, non-writable property: the script must never assign to it or merge onto it, or a strict-mode reassignment throws in the page (measured 2026-09-16, `Script failed to execute`). So the label, tooltip, tokens and anchors arrive on their own plain global `__clawAppSettingsConfig`, which the client sets with an ordinary assignment, and the script only ever READS the bridge.

It is an ARRAY of lines rather than one escaped string, the same shape as prompt-metadata's hook, because a maintainable escape is the only kind that survives an edit: each line here is a line of the script, a diff reads as a diff, and the readers join it with a newline.

The tokens are handed in resolved rather than read from the page, because the affordance is styled to read as part of the footer and the token layer is core/spec/tokens.json's to own. The script falls back to the page's own currentColor and neutral values when a token is absent, so it reads as part of the footer before any theme has been resolved.

The last-resort anchor is the MAIN sidebar shell and no longer anything whose class merely contains "sidebar". Measured 2026-09-16 against a live Control UI: `aside[class*="sidebar"]` also matches `.settings-sidebar`, the settings page's OWN sidebar, so a page that opened on a settings route parked the control at that sidebar's bottom-left corner. Two things followed from that, and both were visible: the control was not in the footer where it belongs, and because the marker made the placement final it stayed there for the life of the page even after the chat layout rendered a real footer. So placement is now re-evaluated on every mutation and the control MOVES to a better anchor when one appears, which is what makes the corner a fallback rather than a destination.

The second click anchor is scoped to the footer strip, matched by the control's ACCESSIBLE NAME, and excludes OUR OWN control. It used to be `[class*="sidebar"] button[class*="settings"]`, which was measured on the same live page pressing `.chat-talk-input-picker__settings`, the chat composer's talk-input settings button, and navigating the reader to /chat/main: a control that does something unrelated is worse than one that does nothing. Its first replacement then had a second bug, caught the same way on 2026-09-16: `[class*="sidebar-footer"] button[aria-label*="settings" i]` also matched the affordance's OWN button, which sits in that footer and is labelled "App settings", so pressing it opened the app's settings and the reader never left. Hence the `:not([data-claw-app-settings])`, and the script skips its own marker as well rather than trusting one selector to be right.

`routes` holds the one Control UI route a client may navigate to, and it is the Control UI's own published path for the destination its own settings entry opens (`onNavigate("appearance")` in components/app-sidebar-agent-menu.ts, whose route table maps `appearance` to `/settings/appearance`). It is used only when there is no control to press at all, which is the state of the Control UI build this was measured against: the footer settings control is newer than the release serving the page. Building a URL was the thing the click was chosen to avoid, so this is second and the click is first; without it the button would silently do nothing, which is the bug class this whole area keeps producing.

Handing the reader to the CONTROL UI's own settings is a different place from this app's settings, and the reason the settings page offers the way there at all. The preferred route is still to CLICK the Control UI's own control rather than to reimplement a navigation: the Control UI owns that route, its control is the shortest path to it, and a client that built the URL itself would be a second copy of a decision that is not ours. Fail soft exactly as placement is: a control that is not there logs and falls through to the route above rather than leaving the reader somewhere invented.

`controlUiSettingsSurface` is what makes the handoff ATOMIC, and it is a SECOND kind of Control UI selector: not where the control is, but what proves the destination has arrived. Measured 2026-09-16: handing the reader to the Control UI's settings is a full document load on the shipping bundle (there is no footer settings control to press, see above), so the client used to dismiss its own surface first and the reader watched the Control UI's PREVIOUS page for the whole load, a visible few seconds, before the settings page painted. Keeping the surface up until this node is painted removes that view entirely instead of covering it, and it is the same shape as the loading cover, which is also only revealed once its page is ready.

It is the settings CONTENT and not the settings shell, and that distinction was measured rather than reasoned: the first version of this used `.settings-sidebar`, and a frame-by-frame capture of the real transition caught the difference. The shell lands at about 3150ms into a load and the panel's own content about 89ms after it, so a readiness answer given on the shell revealed the surface onto a destination that was still painting, and the frames in that window matched neither where the reader had come from nor the destination they were promised. `[role="tabpanel"]` is the panel, so the answer now means the page the reader asked for is DRAWN. It is also an ARIA role rather than a class name, which is the more stable of the two things to depend on in someone else's markup.

The node alone is not enough, which is why the readiness probe also requires the ROUTE. The settings shell is on screen for every `/settings/*` route including the first-run model-setup flow, so a reader who opened app settings from the Control UI's own settings page would satisfy a node-only probe INSTANTLY and be handed straight back into the same non-atomic sequence. Requiring `location.pathname` to equal the destination route is what makes the answer mean 'the page I was asked for has rendered' rather than 'some settings page exists'.

A renamed node fails SOFT in the one direction that matters: the probe stops answering true, the client reveals on its own deadline and logs it, and the reader gets the behaviour of the day before rather than a surface that never lets go. The harness checks this anchor against a live Control UI for exactly that reason, so a rename is caught there rather than in the field.

The two `controlUiSettings` anchors are FLAT strings like the placement ones rather than a nested object, because the phone decodes this file into `[String: String]` and a nested value would fail the whole spec, which fails into an affordance that never installs at all. `controlUiSettingsSurface` is flat for the same reason.
script: try { if (window.console && console.debug) console.debug('[claw] app-settings affordance: ' + message); } catch (e) {}
// The config is a plain global the client sets with an ordinary assignment.
// The bridge is separate and may be a frozen contextBridge object, so it is
if (bridge && typeof bridge.open === 'function') { bridge.open(); return true; }
log('no host bridge to open app settings');
// The one route that never depends on the injected node existing: open() is
// reachable whether or not a button was ever placed, so a page whose footer
// we could not find still has app settings one call away. Set on the config
// global (which is writable) rather than on the frozen bridge. The client
// also has a native fallback of its own (a menu item on the desktop, the
// corner button on iOS); this is the page-side half of that promise.
try { window.__clawAppSettingsConfig = config; config.openAppSettings = open; config.openControlUiSettings = openControlUiSettings; } catch (e) {}
// Hand the reader to the CONTROL UI's own settings, which is a different
// place from this app's settings and the reason our settings page offers the
// way there at all. Driven by CLICKING the Control UI's own footer control,
// so the Control UI keeps owning the route: we ask for the control it already
// has rather than building a URL, which would be a second copy of a decision
// that is not ours. Returns whether a control was there to press.
// Never our own control. It sits in the same footer row, its label is
// "App settings", and pressing it would open the app's settings and
// leave the reader exactly where they were: measured 2026-09-16, when
// the fallback selector matched it. The spec's fallback excludes the
// marker too, and this is the same rule where the marker is understood.
if (control && control.getAttribute && control.getAttribute(MARKER) !== null) control = null;
if (control) { control.click(); log('opened the Control UI settings via ' + targets[i]); return true; }
// No control to press. The Control UI publishes the route its OWN settings
// entry opens, so the reader is taken to that same route rather than left
// where they were: a button that appears to work and does nothing is the
// bug this whole area keeps producing. It is second because it costs a load
// of the page behind our surface, and first place is still the Control UI's
// own control doing its own navigating.
log('no control to press; went to the Control UI route ' + path);
} catch (e) { log('could not navigate to ' + path + ': ' + e); }
log('no Control UI settings control in the footer');
// A gear glyph as inline SVG, so the control carries no dependency on the
// host page's own icon set, which is free to change.
// The best anchor available RIGHT NOW, best first, re-derived on every
// call rather than remembered: the Control UI renders its footer after it
// boots and re-renders it on navigation, so which anchor exists is a fact
// about the page at this moment and not about the page that loaded.
if (actions) return { rank: 3, node: actions, name: 'footer actions', corner: false };
if (footer) return { rank: 2, node: footer, name: 'footer bar (fallback)', corner: false };
if (sidebar) return { rank: 1, node: sidebar, name: 'sidebar corner (last resort)', corner: true };
// Where the control is now, as a rank to compare a better slot against, and
// the node it was put in so a re-render that dropped it is visible.
// In the tree, not merely findable: a re-render replaces the container the
// control was placed in, and a placement that believes it is done is a
// control that is gone until the next reload.
try { return Array.prototype.indexOf.call(placedParent.children, node) !== -1; } catch (e) { return true; }
// Leaving the corner has to clear the corner: `position: absolute` in a
// flex row is a control the footer cannot lay out, and the leftover left
// and bottom would pin it out of the row it was just moved into.
// Place the control, defensively, and keep it in the best place the page
// offers. The primary anchor is the footer's own row of action buttons, where
// it sits beside the Control UI's own controls; the footer bar is the fallback
// if that row is gone, and a sidebar corner is the last resort so the
// affordance is reachable even when the whole footer has been restructured.
// FAIL SOFT: a placement that finds nothing returns false rather than throwing,
// and the client's native route still opens settings.
// It UPGRADES rather than settling. The Control UI opens on whatever route it
// was pointed at, and a page that starts on a settings route has no footer
// action row at all: the footer arrives when the app moves to the chat layout.
// A placement that was final left the control in the last-resort corner for
// the life of the page, which is a fallback that fires permanently and is
// therefore not a fallback. Measured 2026-09-16 on a live Control UI.
} catch (e) { log('ensure threw: ' + e); return false; }
// The footer renders after boot and re-renders on navigation, and a
// re-render can drop our node, so watch for it and put it back. The
// observer is the whole reason a one-shot placement is not enough: the
// Control UI is a single-page app that rebuilds its sidebar.
